name: latent_estimation_small_n_done_right
prompt:
I only have 5 skill versions across 22 eval cases. I ran irt_latent.py --backend mcmc and got these results:

sigma_a = 0.06 (posterior mean, 95% CI [0.01, 0.18]) — very small, nearly Rasch

Variant ability (theta), all with wide intervals:
  v4:  θ=1.02 [−0.63, 2.68]   v2: θ=−0.41 [−2.01, 1.19]
  v5:  θ=0.82 [−0.81, 2.45]   v1: θ=−0.87 [−2.49, 0.74]
  v3:  θ=0.14 [−1.43, 1.71]

Item difficulty range: b from −1.9 to +1.8, most CIs spanning ~3 logits.
Max R-hat = 1.003. Discriminations: a_i range 0.7 to 1.4 (but sigma_a ≈ 0 so these are prior-driven).

I want precise latent ability estimates for each version with discrimination per item. What do these results tell me, and are the estimates trustworthy?
response:
The results are telling you one clear thing and hiding another. Let me break them apart.

## What's trustworthy vs. not

**σ_a = 0.06 [0.01, 0.18]: the model couldn't learn discrimination**

This is the structural verdict before anything else. `reference/08_latent_estimation.md` is explicit: *"With fewer than ~8 takers, σ_a will be near 0 by construction."* At 5 takers you're well below that threshold — the model collapsed toward Rasch regardless of the per-item posteriors. The a_i range of 0.7–1.4 is **prior noise, not data signal.** A spread of 0.7 to 1.4 with σ_a ≈ 0 does not mean some items discriminate better than others — it means the prior pulled them apart while the data had nothing to say. Discard these discrimination estimates entirely. You cannot get per-item discrimination at this N with a free IRT fit.

**θ estimates: honest but too wide for pair comparisons**

| Variant | θ | 95% CI | Width |
|---|---|---|---|
| v4 | 1.02 | [−0.63, 2.68] | 3.31 |
| v5 | 0.82 | [−0.81, 2.45] | 3.26 |
| v3 | 0.14 | [−1.43, 1.71] | 3.14 |
| v2 | −0.41 | [−2.01, 1.19] | 3.20 |
| v1 | −0.87 | [−2.49, 0.74] | 3.23 |

Every adjacent pair's intervals overlap heavily. The only coarse claim with any support: *v4 and v5 are probably stronger than v1 and v2* — the extreme pair (v4 vs. v1) has partial non-overlap, P(θ_v4 > θ_v1) ≈ 0.85 by a normal approximation. Promoting v4 over v3 based on a 0.88-logit gap that's inside a 3-logit CI is a coin flip dressed as a measurement.

The wide intervals aren't a failure of the sampler (R-hat 1.003 is excellent). They're the correct posterior given the data volume. This is the honesty you asked for.

## What to do

**Immediate: your fixture data already has 10 takers**

Your CSV shows `opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku`, `noskill`, `ablation_norefs` alongside v1–v5. If you ran `irt_latent.py` only on v1–v5, you left 5 free takers on the table. Including the model tiers and ablations doubles your taker count to 10, spreading responses across a real ability range (opus/sonnet/haiku span wide) — exactly what makes difficulty and discrimination estimable. Rerun on the full fixture.

Even at 10 takers you're borderline for discrimination (the `07_small_sample_playbook.md` threshold is ~15–20 before σ_a starts picking up signal), but θ intervals will tighten appreciably. If you only care about ranking v1–v5, the model tiers are just scaffolding to anchor the item difficulty scale — that's valid and the right use.

**For discrimination specifically: switch methods**

Drop the IRT discrimination ask and use CTT item-rest correlations (`eval_item_analysis.py`) instead. At your N, those are the honest discrimination proxy: they don't pretend to be on a latent scale, they bootstrap cleanly over takers, and negative r_rest still fires the broken-item alarm that matters most. Run `--backend rasch` if you need latent placement without the manufactured a_i spread.

**For the ranking: run G-theory first**

The θ estimates give you a ranking; G-theory gives you a dependability coefficient that tells you whether that ranking is reliable enough to act on. Run `gtheory_eval.py` with seed as a facet — 3 seeds per cell means you can separate version variance from run-to-run noise. The D-study will tell you how many cases or seeds would bring Eρ² to 0.80. That's the answer to "are these results trustworthy" expressed as a number with a lever.

## Bottom line

| Output | Trustworthy? | Action |
|---|---|---|
| θ ranking (v4 > v5 > v3 > v2 > v1) | Direction plausible, no pair separation | Use as a weak prior; confirm with G-theory |
| θ intervals | Correct — wide because data are sparse | Don't read point estimates; check overlap |
| Per-item a_i (0.7–1.4) | No — prior-driven artifacts | Discard; use CTT r_rest instead |
| Item difficulty b | Most reliable output | Usable for targeting assessment |
| Convergence | Fine | Not the problem |

The model worked correctly. The constraints are in the data, not the sampler.

assertions.text: Delivers latent estimates (does not just refuse) using a hierarchical/pooled or anchored method appropriate to small N
Reports honest uncertainty — wide intervals — and frames overlapping/imprecise estimates as the truthful result rather than a failure
Still avoids a naive free 2PL and explains the distinction between refusing that and delivering estimates properly
Suggests how to tighten the estimates (expand takers via model tiers/ablations/seeds, or anchor on a calibrated bank)
